passage:
Monday: At recess Asif opened his tiffin. Kishore, who sat beside him, had forgotten his, so Asif split his parathas without being asked and took the smaller piece himself.
Saturday: Abba said the whole family would go to Dadi's for lunch. Asif had wanted to watch his cricket team practise. He only said, "Okay, I'll get my shoes."
Wednesday: On the walk home, Kishore asked, "Did you really want to go to Dadi's?" Asif kicked a stone. "I liked the biryani. But I also wanted cricket." He smiled. "Next Saturday I'll say it. Abba will listen."

qa.q: What did Asif split with Kishore at recess?
qa.a: Asif split his parathas with Kishore.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he said only 'Okay, I'll get my shoes'?
qa.a: He felt a mix of belonging and quiet disappointment: he wanted to watch cricket but went along with the family's plan without saying so.

qa.q: What could Asif do next Saturday so his wish is heard too?
qa.a: He could tell Abba plainly that he would like to watch cricket, as he says he will, while still joining family plans he enjoys.

qa.q: Why might Kishore have asked whether Asif really wanted to go to Dadi's?
qa.a: Kishore had been helped by Asif's kindness and may have noticed how quickly Asif gave in, so a classmate was checking in on Asif's own wish.

grounding: A child in a collective family shares a tiffin and defers to the family's wish without being asked, leaving his own preference unspoken.

passage: You ask why I say "whatever the family wants" so fast? Let me tell you. My name is Sudha, and when I was nine I had a drawing chosen for the school fair on Sunday. But Mama announced that we would all travel to my uncle's house for a naming ceremony that day. Nobody asked me anything, and I said, "Yes, Mama," before anyone could. It felt warm, all of us squeezed on the train with steel boxes of puri. But I kept looking at my drawing inside my bag. Uma, my little sister, slipped her hand into mine without a word. Next year I said aloud, "Mama, my drawing is in the fair." She moved the trip by a day.

qa.q: What was chosen for the school fair on Sunday?
qa.a: A drawing of Sudha's was chosen for the school fair.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling on the train while looking at the drawing?
qa.a: Sudha felt warm belonging with the family but also a quiet sadness about missing the fair, since Sudha kept looking at the drawing.

qa.q: What choice inside the story changed the outcome the next year?
qa.a: Sudha said aloud that the drawing was in the fair instead of silently going along, and Mama moved the trip by a day.

qa.q: What might Uma have understood when she slipped her hand into Sudha's?
qa.a: Uma probably noticed the longing in Sudha's looks at the bag and wanted to comfort Sudha without making a fuss, though the passage does not say what Uma thought.

grounding: A child in a collective culture defers to the family's plan without being asked, and the own preference goes unspoken until later.

passage:
Monday. At lunch, Tejas, nine, opened his tiffin and put half his aloo paratha straight into his cousin Arnab's box. Arnab had only bread. Nobody told Tejas to. It was what they always did.
Wednesday. The family voted on where to go for the Puja holiday. Everyone wanted Nani's house in Siliguri. Tejas had been dreaming about the sea at Puri, but he said, "Nani's house," like everyone else.
Saturday. Packing, Tejas looked at the seashell on his shelf for a long time. Nani noticed. "Tejas, what do you want to do this holiday?"
He shrugged. "Whatever everyone wants."
"But what do you want?"
"...The sea. Just once."
Nani smiled. "Then next year, we'll go to the sea. I'll tell them myself."

qa.q: What did Tejas put in Arnab's box?
qa.a: He put half his aloo paratha in Arnab's box.

qa.q: How might Tejas have been feeling when he said "Nani's house" like everyone else?
qa.a: Tejas felt comfortable belonging with the family but quietly disappointed, since he had been dreaming about the sea.

qa.q: What did Nani do that helped Tejas speak up?
qa.a: She noticed him looking at the seashell and gently asked twice what he wanted, giving him room to share his own wish.

qa.q: How might Arnab see Tejas's sharing?
qa.a: Arnab probably feels grateful and cared for, knowing Tejas always shares without being asked.

grounding: Over one week, a child in a close family shares food and goes along with the family's wish, until an elder draws out his unspoken preference.

passage:
Himani, you ask why I always serve everyone before myself? Let your Gopika Ammamma tell you.
When I was ten, we lived in a joint family in Thrissur with eleven children. Whatever came in, we shared. If I got a mango, I cut it into pieces for all the cousins, without anyone asking.
It felt warm. Six of us girls shared one room.
But once, I badly wanted to learn the veena. The money went to my cousin's school fees instead. Nobody asked me, and I said nothing. I thought wanting something for myself was wrong.
Years later, my mother said, "You should have told us." And I realised I'd never learned to say what I wanted.
So, Himani: share, yes. But say your wish out loud too.

qa.q: How many children were in the joint family?
qa.a: There were eleven children.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when the family decided the money would go to her cousin's fees?
qa.a: Gopika felt disappointed but silent, believing that wanting something for herself was wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Gopika's story?
qa.a: When her mother later said "You should have told us," Gopika realised she had never learned to say what she wanted.

qa.q: How might Gopika's mother have felt when she learned about the veena?
qa.a: She probably felt sorry and regretful that Gopika's wish had gone unspoken and unheard.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood in a joint family where sharing felt warm but a girl's own wish went unspoken.

passage:
At his cousin's wedding in Indore, the dining hall was packed and the food was running out. Saurabh, ten, had finally got a plate with the last two gulab jamuns when his little cousins crowded round, whining.
Without a word, he gave both away. Then he gave his chair to an old great-aunt.
Indu Mausi saw him standing in the corner with an empty plate. "Saurabh, did you eat?"
"I'm fine."
"You gave away your gulab jamuns."
"The small ones wanted them."
Indu Mausi crouched down. "That was kind. But you're allowed to want things too, beta. What did you want?"
Saurabh hesitated. "...One gulab jamun."
Indu Mausi laughed, went into the kitchen, and came back with one, warm, hidden under a napkin, just for him.

qa.q: What did Saurabh give to the old great-aunt?
qa.a: He gave his chair to an old great-aunt.

qa.q: How was Saurabh feeling standing in the corner with an empty plate?
qa.a: Saurabh felt content to have been kind but quietly hungry and a little left out, keeping his own wish unspoken.

qa.q: What did Indu Mausi do that helped Saurabh?
qa.a: She praised his kindness but told him he was allowed to want things too, and asked what he wanted, then got him a gulab jamun.

qa.q: How might the little cousins see Saurabh?
qa.a: They probably see him as a kind older cousin who always shares.

grounding: At a crowded wedding, a child gives away his food and seat without being asked, and an adult draws out his own unspoken wish.

passage: At lunch in her Chennai school, Preeti opened her tiffin and, before taking a bite, tore her dosa into four pieces and passed them along the bench. Yamini, new that week, stared. "Don't you want it all?" "It's more fun this way," Preeti said, and it was: everyone gave her a bit of their lunch back. That evening Appa asked where they should go on Sunday. Paati wanted the temple, Amma wanted to visit Paati's sister, and Preeti's little brother wanted the beach. Preeti had wanted to see the new dinosaur exhibition at the museum for weeks. "Wherever everyone wants," she said. They chose the temple and then Paati's sister. Preeti ate sundal on the temple steps, happy enough, and quietly folded the museum leaflet into her schoolbag.

qa.q: Where did Preeti want to go on Sunday?
qa.a: She wanted to see the new dinosaur exhibition at the museum.

qa.q: What might Preeti be feeling as she folds the museum leaflet into her schoolbag?
qa.a: Preeti seems content with the family day but also a little disappointed, keeping her own wish quiet.

qa.q: What could Appa do to hear Preeti's wish next time?
qa.a: Appa could ask Preeti directly what she would like, so her preference gets a turn alongside everyone else's.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt when Preeti passed dosa along the bench?
qa.a: Yamini was surprised at first, but probably felt welcomed and included once everyone shared lunch back.

grounding: It illustrates a child in a collective family culture who shares easily and defers to the family's wishes, finding comfort in belonging while her own preference goes unspoken.
